# AINL few-shot corpus — GENERATED, do not edit.
#
# Built by scripts/build-few-shot.sh from examples/corpus/*.ainl.
# Re-run that script after changing any example; CI checks this file
# is current, so a hand edit here is reverted rather than believed.
#
# This is the prompt-injection source for a model that has never seen
# AINL. Inject SELECTIVELY: every example below is preceded by a header
# naming what it teaches and what it demonstrates, so a request about
# file I/O can be served the file-I/O example without the HTTP or
# modules ones. 'ainl gen --examples <n>' takes the first n; for
# targeted selection, grep for the header line.
#
# Scope: portable examples only. An interpreter-only example is
# excluded because showing it teaches a shape that three of the four
# backends reject outright.

# =====================================================================
# examples/aot-compare.ainl
#   teaches:     while, integer arithmetic, the step cap, AOT parity
#   demonstrates: A compute-heavy loop that runs identically interpreted and AOT-compiled.
# =====================================================================
; @example   aot-compare
; @summary   A compute-heavy loop that runs identically interpreted and AOT-compiled.
; @teaches   while, integer arithmetic, the step cap, AOT parity
; @scope     portable
; @expect    over 400 iterations, loop and fold agree: true
; @run       ainl run examples/corpus/aot-compare.ainl
; @aot       ainl compile examples/corpus/aot-compare.ainl -o /tmp/aot-compare && /tmp/aot-compare
;
; A program whose only job is to do a lot of arithmetic, so the two execution
; backends can be compared directly. This is the shape CI uses for its
; performance gates, and it is worth having in the corpus because "runs on
; the interpreter" and "runs compiled" are different claims.
;
; WHY THIS PROGRAM IS PORTABLE, which is the thing to notice:
;
; Everything it uses — `while`, `def`-rebind, integer `+` and `mod` — is in
; the AOT C runtime AND in all three transpiler targets. `ainl compile`
; emits ONE standalone C program that links against nothing but libc, and the
; AOT builtin table has an id for every one of these. A program that reaches
; for `http-get` or `import` is refused by that backend rather than
; half-supported, so "portable" here is a property you can rely on.
;
; THE STEP CAP. AINL bounds every run at 2,000,000 evaluation steps
; (AINL_MAX_STEPS), so an accidental infinite loop fails loudly with
; "max 2000000 evaluation steps" instead of hanging a CI job. The cap counts
; EVALUATIONS, not iterations, so the loop below — three operations per pass —
; is bounded at roughly 660,000 iterations. Raising the cap for a genuine
; long run is a deliberate act:
;
;     AINL_MAX_STEPS=20000000 ./aot-compare
;
; An AOT binary honors the same variable, so a program that runs under the
; interpreter at a raised cap runs compiled too.

(def n 20000)
(def i 0)
(def checksum 0)

(while (< i n)
  (def checksum (+ checksum (mod (* i 3) 7)))
  (def i (+ i 1)))

(print "iterations:" n)
(print "checksum:" checksum)

; --- the same computation, written differently, must agree -----------------
; A fold and a loop are two spellings of one recursion, and getting the same
; answer from both is a cheap self-check that the loop above is not
; accidentally computing something else. If these two lines ever disagree,
; one of them is wrong — and an AOT binary that disagreed with the
; interpreter would be the far more serious version of that bug.
;
; THE RECURSION DEPTH LIMIT IS 512, and that is a HARD bound on this call
; style: a 20,000-deep fold exceeds it and dies with "recursion limit
; exceeded (max depth 512)". So the fold below is checked at a size that fits,
; and the two computations are run over DIFFERENT ranges on purpose:
;
;   * the `while` loop above handles 20,000 iterations, because a loop's cost
;     is the machine's STACK-FREE — it reuses one frame;
;   * the recursive fold handles only 400, because each nested call costs a
;     frame, and 512 is the ceiling.
;
; This is the single most important practical difference between the two
; styles in AINL, and it is worth stating as a rule: use `while` for anything
; whose length is not known to be small, and recursion for shapes whose depth
; is bounded by the DATA. `fib` at n=20 is fine because 20 frames is nothing;
; a list walk of 20,000 elements is not, and that is the walk `while` is for.
; Note the limit is deliberately NOT reported with a line and column — it
; belongs to the whole run, not to any one form, and a plausible-looking
; wrong line is worse than none (docs/SYNTAX.md 5a).
(def small 400)

(def fold-checksum
  (fn (i acc)
    (if (>= i small) acc
      (fold-checksum (+ i 1) (+ acc (mod (* i 3) 7))))))

(def loop-small
  (fn ()
    (let ((acc 0) (k 0))
      (while (< k small)
        (def acc (+ acc (mod (* k 3) 7)))
        (def k (+ k 1)))
      acc)))

(print "over" small "iterations, loop and fold agree:" (= (loop-small) (fold-checksum 0 0)))

# =====================================================================
# examples/cli-tool.ainl
#   teaches:     env-get, exit, error, or, contains, while, CLI shape
#   demonstrates: A small CLI: read arguments from the environment, validate, process, exit with a code.
# =====================================================================
; @example   cli-tool
; @summary   A small CLI: read arguments from the environment, validate, process, exit with a code.
; @teaches   env-get, exit, error, or, contains, while, CLI shape
; @scope     portable
; @expect    cleaned 3
; @run       ainl run examples/corpus/cli-tool.ainl
;
; The smallest genuinely useful program: arguments in, work, output, exit code.
;
; HOW AN AINL CLI GETS ITS ARGUMENTS — the one thing that surprises everyone
; coming from a language with an `argv`:
;
; AINL HAS NO `argv` BUILTIN. `env-get` is the only channel a program has to
; its caller. So a "command-line tool" reads named environment variables and
; treats each as an optional flag. This is a real trade, not an oversight: a
; real argv would have to be threaded through the interpreter, the bytecode
; VM, the AOT C runtime's `main`, and three transpiler targets, and every one
; of them would have to agree on what "no arguments" means. Environment
; variables are the one input channel that already works identically on all
; four backends.
;
; The consequence to internalize: `env-get` returns `nil` when the variable is
; unset, and nil is FALSEY — so every read needs a default. `(or (env-get "X")
; "d")` is the idiom, and forgetting it is how a CLI ends up doing arithmetic
; on nil. Note that an EMPTY variable and an UNSET one are different values;
; a tool that must tell them apart tests `(= (env-get "X") "")` explicitly.
;
; Try it:
;
;     AINL_TOOL_DIR=examples/corpus ainl run examples/corpus/cli-tool.ainl
;     AINL_TOOL_EXT=.tmp   ainl run examples/corpus/cli-tool.ainl
;
; The defaults below point at a directory this example controls, so the
; program produces the same output on every machine. A CLI example whose
; result depends on whatever happens to be in the working directory is not a
; portable example, and this corpus is checked byte-for-byte on four backends.

; --- argument parsing ------------------------------------------------------
(def dir (or (env-get "AINL_TOOL_DIR") "examples/corpus/libmod"))
(def ext (or (env-get "AINL_TOOL_EXT") ".ainl"))
(def verbose (env-get "AINL_TOOL_VERBOSE"))

; A missing directory is an error from `list-dir` itself, so a tool that wants
; to report it nicely checks first. `file-exists` returns `nil` (not `false`)
; for absence, and true for a file OR a directory.
(if (= (file-exists dir) nil)
  (do
    (print "no such directory:" dir)
    (exit 1))
  nil)

; --- list and filter -------------------------------------------------------
; `list-dir` returns NAMES sorted by byte value, not by locale — that
; ordering is guaranteed on every backend precisely so a program like this
; produces the same output everywhere. (Byte order puts "Capital.txt" before
; "beta.txt", where a locale-aware collation would not.)
(def entries (list-dir dir))
(if verbose (print "verbose: scanned" (len entries) "entries") nil)

; AINL has no `map`/`filter` builtin, so filtering is a plain list walk with a
; predicate. `contains hay needle` is a substring test, which is the right
; tool for "does this name end in the extension I was asked for".
(def keep-entry? (fn (name) (contains name ext)))

(def matching (list))
(def i 0)
(while (< i (len entries))
  (if (keep-entry? (nth entries i))
    (def matching (push matching (nth entries i)))
    nil)
  (def i (+ i 1)))

(print "scanned" (len entries) "entries in" dir)
(print "matching" ext ":" matching)

; --- exit codes are the contract -------------------------------------------
; `exit` ends the process with that status, and it is the only way a program
; tells a shell whether it succeeded:
;
;     if ainl run tool.ainl; then echo ok; fi
;
; A tool that prints an error and then returns NORMALLY exits 0, which tells
; the shell everything worked — the single most common way a script goes wrong.
; So every failure path here exits explicitly, and the success path exits 0.
(if (= (len matching) 0)
  (do
    (print "nothing matched" ext "under" dir)
    (exit 1))
  nil)

; What the tool would actually DO with the matches. This example only reports,
; because deleting files is not something a teaching example should do to
; whatever directory it was pointed at.
(print "would process:" (join matching ", "))
(print "cleaned" (len matching))
(exit 0)

# =====================================================================
# examples/countdown.ainl
#   teaches:     loop, accumulator, def-rebind, print
#   demonstrates: A while loop that accumulates into bindings and prints each step.
# =====================================================================
; examples/corpus/countdown.ainl
; @example   countdown
; @summary   A while loop that accumulates into bindings and prints each step.
; @teaches   loop, accumulator, def-rebind, print
; @scope     portable
; @expect    sum of the steps: 15
;
; `while` does NOT open a scope (docs/SYNTAX.md 2a), so `def` inside the loop
; body rebinds the *enclosing* binding and the mutation sticks. Wrapping the
; body in a `let` would look tidier and silently break the loop: a `let` body
; IS a new scope, so `def` inside it would create a binding that vanishes at
; the end of each iteration.
;
; Run:  ainl run examples/corpus/countdown.ainl

(def n 5)
(def i n)
(def total 0)

(while (> i 0)
  (print "  " i)
  (def total (+ total i))
  (def i (- i 1)))

; `print` space-joins its arguments, so a label ends in NO trailing space —
; `"countdown: " n` would print "countdown:  5", with a double space.
(print "countdown:" n)
(print "sum of the steps:" total)

# =====================================================================
# examples/csv-report.ainl
#   teaches:     split, list, hash, assoc, get, while, the limits of the stdlib
#   demonstrates: Parse a CSV table into records and report counts and a total.
# =====================================================================
; @example   csv-report
; @summary   Parse a CSV table into records and report counts and a total.
; @teaches   split, list, hash, assoc, get, while, the limits of the stdlib
; @scope     portable
; @expect    rows per sku: {"A-1" 2 "B-2" 1}
; @run       ainl run examples/corpus/csv-report.ainl
;
; The most common data job that is not JSON: turn delimited text into records
; and compute something over them.
;
; THREE LIMITS OF THE STDLIB THIS EXAMPLE IS BUILT AROUND. They are stated
; first because each one has a portable answer, and a reader who meets one
; mid-program will think the language is broken rather than bounded.
;
;   1. `split` KEEPS trailing empty fields, so a line ending in a delimiter
;      yields a final "" column. `trim` on every field hides this in ordinary
;      data, which is why it is applied below.
;
;   2. THERE IS NO `str->int` CONVERSION BUILTIN. `(+ "3" 1)` is a type
;      error, and AINL cannot build one from what it has: `nth` takes a LIST,
;      `rest` takes a LIST, and `(split s "")` — the obvious way to get a list
;      of characters — is an EXPLICIT ERROR, because JavaScript would return
;      characters, Rust and C a trailing empty field, and Python would raise.
;      AINL cannot index or iterate a string at all.
;
;      So a numeric field parsed from text stays a STRING, and the aggregate
;      that needs arithmetic runs on values that were integers to begin with.
;      That is not a workaround dressed up as a design; it is the actual
;      boundary, and the two honest responses are to keep numbers as numbers
;      upstream (parse the CSV in a host language and hand AINL a JSON
;      document — see json-payload.ainl) or to add a `str->int` builtin, which
;      would need the same four-backend treatment as the path functions in
;      docs/SYNTAX.md 3.
;
;   3. There is no quote-aware splitter, so a field containing a quoted comma
;      breaks. That is said here rather than papered over: shipping a parser
;      that silently mangles such input is worse than one with a stated limit.

(def csv
  (str "sku,qty,price\n"
       "A-1,2,9.50\n"
       "B-2,5,2.75\n"
       "A-1,1,4.25\n"))

; --- split into lines and fields --------------------------------------------
(def lines (split (trim csv) "\n"))
(def header (split (first lines) ","))
(print "header:" header)
(print "data rows:" (- (len lines) 1))

; --- one row -> a map ------------------------------------------------------
; A record is a MAP keyed by the header names, not a positional list. That is
; what makes the report below readable, and what would make it survive the
; column order changing — a positional record would need the header re-read at
; every access.
;
; `while` does NOT open a scope, so `def row` in the body mutates the `let`'s
; own binding. Wrapping the body in a nested `let` would create a binding
; that vanishes at the end of each iteration, and every record would come back
; EMPTY — silently, and on every backend.
(def to-row
  (fn (fields)
    (let ((row (hash))
          (i 0))
      (while (< i (len header))
        (def row (assoc row (nth header i) (trim (nth fields i))))
        (def i (+ i 1)))
      row)))

(def rows
  (fn (ls)
    (if (< (len ls) 1) (list)
      (cons (to-row (split (first ls) ",")) (rows (rest ls))))))

(def records (rows (rest lines)))
(print "first record:" (first records))
(print "price is still a string:" (get (first records) "price"))

; --- group by a key, with a count ------------------------------------------
; A group-by is a map from key -> count, and `assoc` builds it in one pass
; because it returns a NEW map rather than mutating one. The result's
; insertion order is the order the keys were first seen, which is
; deterministic — so this report is stable across all four backends, and an
; example can assert on its exact text.
(def group-count
  (fn (rs key)
    (if (= (len rs) 0) (hash)
      (let ((k (get (first rs) key))
            (rest-counts (group-count (rest rs) key)))
        (if (has rest-counts k)
          (assoc rest-counts k (+ 1 (get rest-counts k)))
          (assoc rest-counts k 1))))))

(def by-sku (group-count records "sku"))
(print "rows per sku:" by-sku)

; A field-level check, to show that a record is an ordinary map: an absent key
; is `nil`, and `has` is what distinguishes "absent" from "present and nil".
(print "a missing column is nil:" (get (first records) "colour"))
(print "has says so:" (has (first records) "colour"))

; --- where the arithmetic does happen --------------------------------------
; The quantities live in this list as AINL integers, because they were written
; as integers to begin with. A program that RECEIVES numbers in a CSV has to
; keep them as strings, or hand the whole table over as a JSON document —
; which is the real lesson of this example, and the reason the aggregate above
; is a count rather than a sum of the price column.
(def quantities (list 2 5 1))

(def total
  (fn (xs)
    (if (= (len xs) 0) 0
      (+ (first xs) (total (rest xs))))))

(print "total quantity:" (total quantities))

# =====================================================================
# examples/error-handling.ainl
#   teaches:     error, exit, file-exists, error messages, exit codes
#   demonstrates: A program that detects a failure, reports it, and exits with a meaningful code.
# =====================================================================
; @example   error-handling
; @summary   A program that detects a failure, reports it, and exits with a meaningful code.
; @teaches   error, exit, file-exists, error messages, exit codes
; @scope     portable
; @expect    missing: 1
; @run       ainl run examples/corpus/error-handling.ainl
;
; HOW AINL REPORTS FAILURE — read this before writing the next one.
;
; There are two halves to failure, and this example is about the first.
;
; CHECK BEFORE YOU ACT, for a failure you can see coming. A runtime error is
; catchable (`try`/`catch` — see the `try-catch` example beside this one), but
; catching is not the same as testing. A check is cheaper, states the intent
; directly, and keeps the failure out of the control flow:
;
;     (read-file p)            raises on a missing file
;     (file-exists p)          returns nil  <- ask this first
;
;     (json-parse s)           raises on malformed text
;     ...                      validate before you parse
;
;     (nth xs 99)              returns nil for an out-of-range index (no raise)
;
;     (get h "missing")        returns nil (no raise)
;
; So: prefer builtins that return `nil` over builtins that raise, and when you
; must use a raising builtin, guard it with a check. `(if (file-exists p) ... )`
; is not defensive noise — it is the clearest way to express "if this is
; there", and it does not cost a handler.
;
; Two kinds of failure, handled differently:
;
;   EXPECTED  — a missing file, a malformed payload. Check first, report,
;               continue or exit deliberately. This is what this example does.
;   IMPOSSIBLE — a broken invariant, a bug. Call `error`, which aborts
;               immediately. Do not try to carry on past it.
;
; And for an expected failure you genuinely cannot check for in advance — a
; connection that may drop mid-flight, a parse of text whose validity you only
; learn by attempting it — `try`/`catch` is the tool, not a last resort. The
; line is not "never catch"; it is "know whether the check or the catch is the
; honest description of this failure".

(def path "ainl-corpus-does-not-exist.txt")

; --- the expected failure: a check, then a decision -----------------------
; `file-exists` returns `nil` (not `false`) for absence, and that is
; deliberate: it is tested the same way as a missing map key, with
; `(= (file-exists p) nil)`. `nil` is falsey, so `(if (file-exists p) ...)`
; works too, and that is what a reader expects.
(def present (file-exists path))
(print "exists?" present)

(if (= present nil)
  (do
    (print "missing:" 1)
    (print "the program continues — it did not die on a missing file")
    nil)
  nil)

; --- the same check, but for a case that IS an error -----------------------
; Here the file DOES exist — this program is running from the repository
; root, and this very file is there. So a missing file would mean something
; the program cannot explain: a bug, or a path it does not control. `error`
; aborts with a diagnostic and a non-zero exit, which is exactly right for
; that, because continuing would mean processing data the program never
; verified.
;
; The point being made is the shape: the `if` is FALSE here, so `error` does
; not run and the program carries on. Written the other way round — erroring
; whenever a check fails, without asking whether the failure is expected —
; this is the program that dies on the first missing file and never reaches
; the rest of its work.
(def self (env-get "AINL_SELF"))
(if (and (not (= self nil)) (= (file-exists self) nil))
  (error "this program is running but its own source is missing")
  nil)

; The same guard, against a file the program cannot control, is the one to
; write on. It does not run, because the path is intentionally absent.
(if (= (file-exists "no-such-dir-anywhere/never.txt") nil)
  (do
    (print "and a check that passes leaves the program alone")
    nil)
  nil)

; --- what an error message looks like --------------------------------------
; An uncaught runtime error is written to stderr and exits 1:
;
;   <kind> error: <what went wrong> at line N, col M (byte B) — did you mean 'x'?
;
; The four shapes are: unbound symbol, arity mismatch, type error, parse
; error. Columns count CHARACTERS, not bytes, so they line up with an editor.
; The `— did you mean 'x'?` suggestion appears when a close name is in scope,
; which turns a failed run into a single edit. Two errors deliberately carry
; no position: resource limits (they belong to the whole run, not one form) and
; the AOT C / transpiler backends (they embed no source, so a line does not
; exist to point at). See docs/SYNTAX.md 5a.

; --- exiting deliberately --------------------------------------------------
; A program that prints an error and then returns NORMALLY still exits 0,
; which tells every shell and CI job that it succeeded. `exit` is the only way
; to set the status deliberately, so a tool that can fail should always end in
; an explicit `exit`.
;
; Below, the run succeeds and exits 0. Run the failing variant yourself with:
;
;   printf '(error "deliberate")\n' > /tmp/e.ainl && ainl run /tmp/e.ainl; echo $?
;
(print "handled 1 expected failure and exited cleanly")
(exit 0)

# =====================================================================
# examples/file-roundtrip.ainl
#   teaches:     file-io, read-file, write-file, delete-file, file-exists, string
#   demonstrates: Read a file, transform its contents, and write it back out.
# =====================================================================
; @example   file-roundtrip
; @summary   Read a file, transform its contents, and write it back out.
; @teaches   file-io, read-file, write-file, delete-file, file-exists, string
; @scope     portable
; @expect    normalized: AINL IS A LIST OF FORMS
; @run       ainl run examples/corpus/file-roundtrip.ainl
;
; The everyday shape: a program that owns a file it produced itself.
;
; WHERE THE FILE GOES, and why it is a fixed relative path:
;
;   * AINL has no notion of a current directory, so the program names the
;     path explicitly.
;   * `write-file` does NOT create parent directories. A missing directory is
;     a `write-file: cannot write` error, not a silent mkdir — so the path
;     must name a directory that already exists.
;   * The name is FIXED, not derived from `env-get "TMPDIR"`. A corpus
;     example's output is compared byte-for-byte against three transpiler
;     targets and re-run on every CI job; a path containing a per-user
;     temporary directory would make the output machine-dependent and turn
;     that comparison into a coin flip. The path below lands in the repository
;     root, which exists, and the program deletes the file before exiting, so
;     a run leaves nothing behind.
;
; The cleanup is not optional. An example that leaks a file makes the checkout
; dirty on every run, and a corpus people stop running is a corpus that stops
; teaching.

(def path "ainl-corpus-file-roundtrip.tmp")

; --- write -----------------------------------------------------------------
; A file's content is ONE string; newlines are ordinary characters inside it.
; Nothing here "adds a line" — the program builds a string containing
; newlines and the runtime writes those bytes exactly as they are.
(write-file path (str "  ainl  is  a  list  of  forms\n"
                      "the  second  line  has  double  spaces\n"
                      "  and the third is indented\n"))
(print "wrote 3 lines to" path)

; --- read back -------------------------------------------------------------
; The bytes just written are valid UTF-8 by construction, so `read-file`
; returns a str and the round trip is byte-exact: the leading spaces on the
; first and third lines are still there.
(print "leading spaces survive the round trip:"
       (first (split (read-file path) "\n")))

; --- transform -------------------------------------------------------------
; AINL cannot index a string (`(nth "abc" 1)` is an error — `nth` takes a
; list), so text processing is `split` plus list operations. Here: split into
; lines, trim each, drop the empties, upper-case.
;
; THREE THINGS THAT MAKE THIS CORRECT, all of them easy to get wrong:
;
;   1. `split` KEEPS trailing empty fields, so a file ending in "\n" yields a
;      final "" element. The `(= (trim w) "")` guard removes it. Without it,
;      the last line of every real file is a blank one.
;
;   2. `while` does NOT open a scope, so `def` in the body mutates the `let`'s
;      own bindings. Wrapping the body in a nested `let` would create a
;      binding that vanishes at the end of each iteration, and `out` would
;      come back empty — silently, and on every backend.
;
;   3. `replace s "  " " "` is NOT a whitespace collapser, and this example
;      does not pretend otherwise. It rewrites non-overlapping occurrences
;      left to right, so four spaces become TWO, not one — one pass does not
;      converge, and AINL has no regex to say "a run of whitespace" instead.
;      What it does do is collapse the DOUBLE spaces this sample actually
;      contains, and `trim` removes whatever the ends still carry. If you
;      genuinely need runs collapsed, the honest AINL answer is `split` on " "
;      and `join` with " " — which drops the empty fields that runs produce.
;      That is a two-liner, and it is the shape used in flatten-lines.ainl.

(def raw (split (read-file path) "\n"))
(def out (list))
(def i 0)
(while (< i (len raw))
  (def w (trim (replace (nth raw i) "  " " ")))
  (if (= (trim w) "")
    nil
    (def out (push out (upcase w))))
  (def i (+ i 1)))

(print "normalized:" (join out " | "))

; --- write it back ---------------------------------------------------------
(write-file path (str (join out "\n") "\n"))
(print "first line after rewriting:" (first (split (read-file path) "\n")))

; --- clean up --------------------------------------------------------------
; `delete-file` errors on a directory and on a missing path, so it is only
; safe here because this program definitely just created the file. `file-exists`
; returns `nil` (not `false`) for absence, which is why it prints as nil below.
(delete-file path)
(print "cleaned up; the file exists now?" (file-exists path))

# =====================================================================
# examples/flatten-tree.ainl
#   teaches:     recursion, higher-order, list, fn
#   demonstrates: A recursive function that flattens a nested list, plus map/filter/reduce written in AINL.
# =====================================================================
; @example   flatten-tree
; @summary   A recursive function that flattens a nested list, plus map/filter/reduce written in AINL.
; @teaches   recursion, higher-order, list, fn
; @scope     portable
; @expect    flattened: (1 2 3 4 5 6)
; @run       ainl run examples/corpus/flatten-tree.ainl
;
; Two different recursion styles, side by side, because real AINL uses both:
;
;   1. `flatten` recurses on a *structurally recursive* value — a value that is
;      either an atom or a list of such values, to any depth. A tree is not
;      just "a list", and a shape that never nests needs no case for nesting.
;
;   2. `map1`/`filter1`/`reduce` recurse on a *flat* list with a base case on
;      `(len l) = 0`. This is the shape you will write most often, and it is
;      AINL's stand-in for the iteration a language with a `for` would give
;      you. All three take a function as an argument, which is what makes
;      them reusable instead of three hardcoded loops.
;
; THE ONE TRICK IN HERE, and the reason the tree below can hold bare numbers:
; AINL has NO `list?` type predicate. `(len 5)` and `(has 5 "k")` are type
; errors, not `false` — so the obvious generic walker, which asks "is this
; element a list or a number?", cannot be written directly.
;
; What *does* work, and is exact on all four backends, is testing the JSON
; spelling of the value: a list serializes to something starting with "[",
; an atom to something starting with "{", a digit, a quote or a letter. So
;
;     (def listy? (fn (x) (= (first (split (json-serialize x) "[")) "")))
;
; is a working, portable `list?`. It costs a serialization per element, which
; is why you should reach for it only when the shape genuinely is recursive —
; for a flat list, `(len l)` is the whole story and you never need this.
; (An AOT binary behaves the same here; note that `ainl compile` does not
; type-check, it generates code that fails at run time, so "AOT compiled
; successfully" is never evidence that a program is correct.)

; --- 1. recursion over a nested structure ----------------------------------
; A portable `list?`, built from the JSON spelling. Splitting on "[" is the
; trick: for a list the string starts with the separator, so the part before
; it is the empty string; for anything else it is the value's own text.
(def listy?
  (fn (x) (= (first (split (json-serialize x) "[")) "")))

; AINL has no `append` builtin, and this is the one you will write first.
; `cons` prepends and `push` appends *values* to a list, so neither can join
; two lists of unknown length. This walks `a` and conses each element onto
; the recursion, which puts the elements back in their original order.
(def append
  (fn (a b)
    (if (= (len a) 0) b
      (cons (first a) (append (rest a) b)))))

(print "append:" (append (list 1 2) (list 3 4 5)))

; The base case is "no elements left". Otherwise: if the head is itself a
; list, flatten it and put it in front; if it is an atom, keep it in front.
; Note the argument order: `cons` takes the VALUE first and the list second,
; so everything here builds right-to-left.
(def flatten
  (fn (xs)
    (if (= (len xs) 0) (list)
      (if (listy? (first xs))
        (append (flatten (first xs)) (flatten (rest xs)))
        (cons (first xs) (flatten (rest xs)))))))

; A mixed tree, exactly the shape that cannot be written without `listy?`:
; atoms and lists side by side, nested three deep.
(def tree (list 1 (list 2 3) (list (list 4) 5) 6))

(print "tree:     " tree)
(print "flattened:" (flatten tree))

; A flat list is the same function with no nesting at all — which is why
; `listy?` costs more than it looks, and why a flat list should just use it.
(def flat (list 1 2 3))
(print "flat:     " (flatten flat))

; --- 2. map / filter / reduce, all in AINL ---------------------------------
; Higher-order means a function is an ordinary value: it can be passed,
; returned and stored. There is no lambda syntax to learn — `(fn (x) ...)` is
; the value.
(def map1
  (fn (f xs)
    (if (= (len xs) 0) (list)
      (cons (f (first xs)) (map1 f (rest xs))))))

(def filter1
  (fn (pred xs)
    (if (= (len xs) 0) (list)
      (if (pred (first xs))
        (cons (first xs) (filter1 pred (rest xs)))
        (filter1 pred (rest xs))))))

; `reduce` is the one with an accumulator, and the accumulator is an ordinary
; second parameter — the starting value is the *argument*, not the parameter.
(def reduce1
  (fn (f init xs)
    (if (= (len xs) 0) init
      (reduce1 f (f init (first xs)) (rest xs)))))

(def nums (list 1 2 3 4 5 6))
(print "kept:    " (filter1 (fn (n) (= (mod n 2) 0)) nums))
(print "doubled: " (map1 (fn (n) (* n 2)) nums))
(print "total:   " (reduce1 (fn (acc n) (+ acc n)) 0 nums))

; The three compose, which is the point of taking functions as arguments.
(print "sum of the evens:" (reduce1 (fn (a n) (+ a n)) 0
                                     (filter1 (fn (n) (= (mod n 2) 0)) nums)))

# =====================================================================
# examples/json-payload.ainl
#   teaches:     json-parse, json-serialize, hash, get, keys, list, fn
#   demonstrates: Parse an API-shaped JSON payload, extract fields, and re-serialize a summary.
# =====================================================================
; @example   json-payload
; @summary   Parse an API-shaped JSON payload, extract fields, and re-serialize a summary.
; @teaches   json-parse, json-serialize, hash, get, keys, list, fn
; @scope     portable
; @expect    summary: {"count":2,"units":7}
; @run       ainl run examples/corpus/json-payload.ainl
;
; The shape almost every real AINL program has: a JSON document arrives as a
; string, becomes a value, gets read, and leaves as a string.
;
; WHAT JSON BECOMES. The reader is hand-written in every backend rather than
; mapped onto the host's JSON library, and it is a strict, unsurprising
; mapping (docs/SYNTAX.md 3):
;
;     object -> hash (a map), keys in INSERTION order
;     array  -> list
;     string -> str    number -> int or float    true/false -> true/false
;     null   -> nil
;
; Two consequences shape the code below. A parsed object is an ordinary AINL
; map, so `get` is the only access syntax you ever need — no dotted paths, no
; field syntax, and a nested object is reached with a nested `get`. And
; because a map's equality is insertion-order-sensitive, re-serializing a
; parsed object is idempotent in the way that matters: parse, write, parse
; again and you get an equal value, because the order survived.

(def payload
  (json-parse
    (str "{\"page\": 1, \"items\": ["
         "{\"sku\": \"A-1\", \"name\": \"widget\", \"qty\": 2, \"price\": 9.5},"
         "{\"sku\": \"B-2\", \"name\": \"gadget\", \"qty\": 5, \"price\": 2.75}"
         "], \"meta\": {\"total\": 2}, \"cursor\": null}")))

; --- reading nested fields --------------------------------------------------
(print "page:" (get payload "page"))
(print "meta.total:" (get (get payload "meta") "total"))
; A key that is absent is `nil`, and a JSON `null` is ALSO `nil` — the two are
; indistinguishable. That is a real limit of the mapping, and a program that
; must tell "missing" from "explicitly null" cannot use this representation.
(print "cursor:" (get payload "cursor") "(absent key gives the same:) " (get payload "nope"))

(def items (get payload "items"))
(print "items:" items)
(print "first item's name:" (get (first items) "name"))

; --- walking a list of records ---------------------------------------------
; A parsed array is a plain list, so the ordinary list operations apply with no
; JSON-specific code at all. AINL has no `map` builtin, so the fold is written
; out; the accumulator is a second parameter, not a special closure.
(def total-units
  (fn (rows)
    (if (= (len rows) 0) 0
      (+ (get (first rows) "qty")
         (total-units (rest rows))))))

(print "total units:" (total-units items))

; --- building a new document -----------------------------------------------
; `(hash k v ...)` builds a map; insertion order is what `json-serialize`
; prints, so the order here IS the order in the output. This is why a
; hand-built document and a re-serialized one can be compared byte-for-byte.
(def summary (hash "count" (len items) "units" (total-units items)))
(def out (json-serialize summary))
(print "summary:" out)

; --- the round trip ---------------------------------------------------------
; Re-parsing what we serialized gives a value equal to the one we built. This
; is the property that makes it safe to hand a document to another system: the
; text and the value agree.
(def reparsed (json-parse out))
(print "round trip is equal:" (= reparsed summary))
(print "the original still parses cleanly:" (= (get (json-parse (json-serialize payload)) "page") 1))

# =====================================================================
# examples/try-catch.ainl
#   teaches:     try, catch, error, get, error messages
#   demonstrates: Handling a failure that CAN happen, without dying.
# =====================================================================
; @example   try-catch
; @summary   Handling a failure that CAN happen, without dying.
; @teaches   try, catch, error, get, error messages
; @scope     portable
; @expect    reached the end without dying
; @run       ainl run examples/corpus/try-catch.ainl
;
; CATCHING A FAILURE THAT CAN HAPPEN.
;
; The example beside this one, `error-handling`, is about failures you should
; AVOID: check before you act, and reserve `error` for a broken invariant. This
; one is the other half — the failure you EXPECT and must carry on past.
;
; A runtime error is catchable:
;
;     (try body... (catch (e) handler...))
;
; If `body` succeeds its value is the value of the whole form. If it raises,
; `e` is bound to the error, the handler runs, and ITS value is the value of
; the whole form. So `try` is an ordinary expression, and the natural way to
; write it is to bind the result:
;
;     (def status (try (risky-thing) (catch (e) "fallback")))
;
; `e` is a map with two keys, in this order: "message" (a string) and "kind"
; (the string "runtime"). The order is part of the contract — every backend
; prints a map in insertion order, so `message` first is what makes a caught
; value print identically everywhere.

; --- the smallest useful catch --------------------------------------------
; Division by zero is a runtime error, and it is the clearest demonstration:
; the body cannot produce a value at all, so only the handler can.
;
; The success case uses `+` rather than `/` deliberately. AINL's `/` is float
; division and JavaScript has only one number type, so `(/ 10 2)` prints 5.0 on
; four backends and 5 on the fifth — a known, pre-existing divergence that this
; example is marked `portable` and must not rest on. The caught-error line
; below is unaffected: the division never produces a value to print.
(print "1+2 =" (try (+ 1 2) (catch (e) "unreachable")))
(print "10/0 =" (try (/ 10 0) (catch (e) (str "caught: " (get e "message")))))

; A caught error is a NORMAL VALUE. It can be stored, carried and read later,
; which is what makes `try` usable as a building block and not just a guard.
(def saved (try (error "the disk is full") (catch (e) e)))
(print "stored:" (get saved "message") "kind:" (get saved "kind"))

; --- the pattern: a value or a reason -------------------------------------
; This is the ordinary shape — attempt the operation, and if it cannot be done,
; return a stated alternative instead of propagating. Reading a file is the
; canonical case, because a missing file is an expected outcome of any program
; that takes a path from a user, not a malfunction.
(def path "ainl-corpus-does-not-exist.txt")

(def contents
  (try (read-file path)
       (catch (e) nil)))

(if (= contents nil)
  (do
    (print "could not read" path "->" (get (try (read-file path) (catch (e) e)) "message"))
    nil)
  (print "read" (len contents) "bytes"))

; Note the shape above: the FALLBACK is `nil`, and the diagnostic is computed
; separately. That is deliberate. If the handler had to both report and produce
; a usable value, a caller would have to unwrap a two-field result to find out
; whether the operation worked — and a string that reads like a message is
; indistinguishable from data. Return the value you want; report separately.

; --- one catch, many attempts ----------------------------------------------
; Because a `try` is an expression, a loop body can contain several and the
; loop simply continues. This is the shape a health check or a batch import
; needs: a failure on item N must not cost you items N+1..n.
(def paths (list "a-missing-file.txt" "another-missing.txt" "still-missing"))
(def results (list))
(def i 0)
(while (< i (len paths))
  (def p (nth paths i))
  (def outcome (try (read-file p)
                   (catch (e) (str "FAILED: " (get e "message")))))
  (def results (push results outcome))
  (def i (+ i 1)))
(print "batch:" results)
(print "reached the end without dying")

; --- nesting: the innermost catch wins -------------------------------------
; When a `try` is inside another `try`, the inner handler sees the error first
; and the outer one never runs — unless the inner handler itself raises, in
; which case the error propagates OUT to the outer `catch`.
(print "nested:"
  (try (try (error "inner")
            (catch (e) (str "inner handled: " (get e "message"))))
       (catch (e) "outer must not run")))

; --- when NOT to catch -----------------------------------------------------
; `catch` is for a failure the program can meaningfully continue past. It is
; not a way to make a bug quiet: swallowing an error you did not expect leaves
; a program that runs to completion having done nothing useful, and the
; diagnostic is the only thing that would have told you. A broken invariant
; should still call `error` and exit non-zero — see `error-handling`.
;
; That is the whole discipline: `try` for the expected, `error` for the
; impossible, and a check before either when the check is cheap.
(print "done")
(exit 0)

# =====================================================================
# examples/word-frequency.ainl
#   teaches:     while, let, def-rebind, list, hash, assoc, selection sort
#   demonstrates: Tokenize a text, count the words, and report the most frequent ones.
# =====================================================================
; @example   word-frequency
; @summary   Tokenize a text, count the words, and report the most frequent ones.
; @teaches   while, let, def-rebind, list, hash, assoc, selection sort
; @scope     portable
; @expect    most frequent: ("alpha" 4)
; @run       ainl run examples/corpus/word-frequency.ainl
;
; The single most common real AINL shape: split some text, count it, report
; it. Everything here is list and map operations — no I/O, no server.

(def text "alpha beta alpha gamma beta alpha delta alpha epsilon beta")

; --- tokenize --------------------------------------------------------------
; `split` keeps TRAILING empty fields, so the empty guard is not optional: a
; text ending in a space would otherwise contribute a final "" word.
; `trim` removes the whitespace at each end and `downcase` folds case, so
; "Alpha" and "alpha" are one word.
;
; `while` does NOT open a scope, so `def` in the body mutates the `let`'s own
; bindings. Wrapping the body in a nested `let` would create a binding that
; vanishes at the end of each iteration, and this function would return an
; empty list — silently, on every backend.
(def tokenize
  (fn (t)
    (let ((raw (split (trim (replace t "\n" " ")) " "))
           (out (list))
           (i 0))
      (while (< i (len raw))
        (def w (trim (nth raw i)))
        (if (= w "") nil (def out (push out (downcase w))))
        (def i (+ i 1)))
      out)))

(def words (tokenize text))
(print "tokens:" (len words))
(print words)

; --- count -----------------------------------------------------------------
; `assoc` returns a NEW map rather than mutating one, so the accumulator is
; threaded through the recursion and returned. There is no mutable map to
; update in place; `def`-ing the map inside a loop body would just rebind the
; local to a fresh value each time and lose the count.
(def count-words
  (fn (ws)
    (if (= (len ws) 0) (hash)
      (let ((w (first ws))
            (seen (count-words (rest ws))))
        (if (has seen w)
          (assoc seen w (+ 1 (get seen w)))
          (assoc seen w 1))))))

(def counts (count-words words))
(print "distinct:" (len (keys counts)))
(print "counts:" counts)

; --- from a map to sortable pairs ------------------------------------------
; A (word, count) pair is just a two-element list: `first` is the word and
; `nth p 1` is the count. AINL has no tuples and no `sort`, so this is the
; shape to reach for whenever a map has to be ordered by its values.
(def to-pairs
  (fn (h)
    (let ((ks (keys h))
           (out (list))
           (i 0))
      (while (< i (len ks))
        (def out (push out (list (nth ks i) (get h (nth ks i)))))
        (def i (+ i 1)))
      out)))

; --- selection sort, by count descending -----------------------------------
; For each position, find the pair with the largest count and swap it there.
; The swap needs an explicit remove-then-insert, because AINL has no
; list-slicing or index-assignment builtin — `remove-at` and `insert-at` are
; the two primitives a sort needs, and a general program ends up writing both.
(def remove-at
  (fn (xs i)
    (let ((out (list))
           (k 0))
      (while (< k (len xs))
        (if (= k i) nil (def out (push out (nth xs k))))
        (def k (+ k 1)))
      out)))

(def insert-at
  (fn (xs i v)
    (let ((out (list))
           (k 0))
      (while (< k (len xs))
        (if (= k i) (def out (push out v)) nil)
        (def out (push out (nth xs k)))
        (def k (+ k 1)))
      (if (>= i (len xs)) (push out v) out))))

; THE SCOPING TRAP, made concrete. This sort needs three loop variables, and
; the obvious way to write it is to open a `let` for the inner two:
;
;     (while (< i n)
;       (let ((best i) (j 0))        ; <-- WRONG
;         ...))
;
; A `let` body IS A NEW SCOPE (docs/SYNTAX.md 2a), so every `def out` inside
; it creates a binding that VANISHES at the end of the iteration. The sort
; then returns its input completely unchanged, with no error, on every
; backend — the worst possible failure, because it looks like it worked.
;
; `while` itself does NOT open a scope, so the fix is to keep the whole body
; FLAT and declare `best` and `j` in the same `let` as `out` and `i`, before
; the loop. That is also why the existing project examples write their loop
; bodies flat. The rule: use one `let` for the whole function, and `do` (which
; does not open a scope either) purely to group.
(def sort-by-count
  (fn (ps)
    (let ((n (len ps))
           (out ps)
           (i 0)
           (best 0)
           (j 0)
           (held-i nil)
           (held-best nil))
      (while (< i n)
        (def best i)
        ; THE SCAN STARTS AT `i`, NOT AT 0. Position 0 already holds the
        ; largest count from the previous pass, so a scan from 0 immediately
        ; re-finds it, sets `best` to 0, and then `(> best i)` is false for
        ; every remaining i — the loop runs to completion having done nothing
        ; after the first pass. Selection sort over a suffix is the whole
        ; algorithm: positions before `i` are already final and must not be
        ; considered again.
        (def j i)
        (while (< j n)
          ; STRICT `>`, not `>=`: on a tie the earlier element stays the
          ; maximum, so the sort is STABLE and the output is deterministic.
          ; A sort whose result depends on strict-versus-non-strict is a sort
          ; whose output can differ between backends, and this corpus is
          ; compared byte-for-byte on four of them.
          (if (> (nth (nth out j) 1) (nth (nth out best) 1))
            (def best j)
            nil)
          (def j (+ j 1)))
        (if (> best i)
          (do
            ; Hold BOTH values BEFORE removing anything: reading `(nth out
            ; best)` from a list that has already had an element removed gets
            ; whatever shifted into that slot.
            (def held-i (nth out i))
            (def held-best (nth out best))
            (def out (remove-at out i))
            ; `best - 1`, because the removal above shifted every later index
            ; down by one.
            (def out (remove-at out (- best 1)))
            (def out (insert-at out i held-best))
            (def out (insert-at out best held-i)))
          nil)
        (def i (+ i 1)))
      out)))

(def ranked (sort-by-count (to-pairs counts)))
(print "ranked:" ranked)
(print "most frequent:" (first ranked))

; Every word that appears more than once, which is the query a real report
; wants. `filter` is a list walk with a predicate — AINL has no builtin for
; it, so this is the shape to reuse.
(def frequent
  (fn (ps)
    (if (= (len ps) 0) (list)
      (if (> (nth (first ps) 1) 1)
        (cons (first ps) (frequent (rest ps)))
        (frequent (rest ps))))))

(print "appearing twice or more:" (frequent ranked))
